summary: A paper surveying useful information and file repositories available on the network for end users, in the style of a treasure-hunting guide. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1402.

eli5.summary: A treasure map for the early Internet. It points to places on the network where you could find useful files and information, back when there was no easy search engine.

questions: finding information on the early internet
how did people search the early internet
what was an early internet resource guide
how to use archie and ftp
subtitle: A practical guide to finding information and resources on the early Internet.

tldr.problem: By 1991, vast amounts of useful information existed on the Internet, but there was no search engine. Users had to know where to look and how to navigate using Telnet, FTP, and other tools. The challenge was finding and cataloging resources scattered across thousands of computers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1290 provides a comprehensive guide to the major information sources on the early Internet, including library catalogs, software repositories, network resource guides, campus information systems, bulletin boards, and directory services, with detailed instructions for accessing each via FTP, Telnet, and other methods.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1290 was replaced by RFC 1402, as web search engines and the World Wide Web eventually made dedicated resource guides obsolete.

today: RFC 1402 replaced RFC 1290, as the World Wide Web and search engines eventually made this resource guide obsolete. However, RFC 1290 stands as a snapshot of how people found information on the early Internet before Google and web browsers became dominant.

sections.title: The Information Problem on the Early Internet
sections.content:
By December 1991, the Internet contained an enormous wealth of information: library catalogs, software archives, technical documents, databases, and more. However, finding information was difficult. There was no search engine like Archie or the Web; instead, users had to know the address of a server, understand file systems, and use command-line tools.

RFC 1290 addresses three core problems: First, how do people know information exists? Second, even if they know, how do they know if it is important or relevant to their field? Third, once they know what they want, how do they find and retrieve it? The RFC argues that librarians and information professionals need a reference guide to point users to these sources.
sections.eli5: In 1991, the Internet had a lot of information, but no easy way to search it. This RFC says: here are lists of where to find things, how to fetch them with FTP, and what you can expect to find.

sections.title: Resource Guides, Indexes, and Bibliographies
sections.content:
The RFC describes a number of documents that index network resources:

  • The Internet Resource Guide, available from NNSC.NSF.NET, was a comprehensive guide to computational resources, library catalogs, archives, and networks. It could be accessed via FTP (as compressed PostScript or ASCII) or by Telnet to the Colorado Alliance of Research Libraries (pac.carl.org), which allowed keyword searching.
  • The Anonymous FTP Sites list was maintained on pilot.njin.net; users could also search it with Archie (a tool accessed via Telnet to quiche.cs.mcgill.ca), which let them search for specific programs or files.
  • Several RFCs provided pointers: RFC 1118 (Hitchhiker's Guide), RFC 1175 (Bibliography of Internetworking Information), RFC 1206 and RFC 1207 (Frequently Asked Questions), and RFC 1208 (Networking Glossary).
  • The Interest Groups List from NISC.SRI.COM told users about mailing lists and discussion groups.
sections.eli5: The RFC lists several documents that already existed on the network that cataloged resources. For example, the Internet Resource Guide was like a card catalog, and Archie was a tool that could search for specific files across FTP sites.

sections.title: Libraries, Software Archives, and Network Information Centers
sections.content:
The RFC covers several categories of resources:

  • Library Catalogs: Hundreds of libraries offered Telnet access to their catalogs. Two major guides cataloged them: "Internet-Accessible Library Catalogs and Databases" (by Art St. George and Ron Larsen) and "UNT's Accessing On-Line Bibliographic Databases" (by Billy Barron). These could be retrieved via FTP.
  • Anonymous FTP Sites: Washington University (wuarchive.wustl.edu) was a major software mirror with a copy of the Simtel20 archive, containing hundreds of programs for DOS and Macintosh. Kermit (file transfer software) was available from Columbia University. NCSA provided Telnet and network access software for PCs and Macs.
  • Network Information Centers (NICs): The RFC lists contact information for the Defense Data Network NIC, NSF Network Service Center, NSFNET Information Services, and others. These were the human institutions that provided network information and could connect new users to the Internet.
sections.eli5: The RFC points to libraries where you could search for books (via Telnet), software repositories where you could download programs, and people (the NICs) who could answer questions about how to get connected.

sections.title: Campus Wide Information Systems (CWIS) and Bulletin Boards
sections.content:
Universities were building Campus Wide Information Systems (CWIS)—menu-driven systems that made network resources invisible to the end user. The RFC describes over 25 examples:

  • Cornell's CUINFO (cuinfo.cornell.edu, port 300) offered a "Uncle Ezra" electronic counselor, student directories, ski reports, job listings, computing information, patents, and weather.
  • MIT's TechInfo (techinfo.mit.edu) provided a menu system with source code available to other universities.
  • Ohio State's system and many others offered similar local information on calendars, directories, and resources.

The RFC also describes bulletin board systems and Freenets like Cleveland Freenet (freenet-in-a.cwru.edu), which were free, anonymous services open to the public. It lists specialized services like FEDIX (federal research funding information), STIS (NSF publications), and geographic name servers that let you query information by city and state.
sections.eli5: Universities built menus so students and staff could access all their information without remembering command lines. There were also public bulletin boards you could call up on the network, like digital town squares. Some specialized systems let you search for federal funding, NSF research, or geographic information.

sections.title: WHOIS, Finger, and Email Directories
sections.content:
For finding people, the RFC describes WHOIS and finger services, early versions of email directories. WHOIS (accessible via Telnet or the whois command) allowed you to search a database of people at a site by name and get their contact information. Different universities had their own WHOIS servers with varying search formats.

The RFC lists WHOIS servers at Ohio State, University of Oregon, University of Virginia, MIT, Indiana University, and others. Each had a slightly different interface and naming convention (some used firstname.lastname, others used lastname, firstname). This lack of standardization shows the Internet before unified email directories, when each institution maintained its own.
sections.eli5: Before email directories, each university ran its own white pages. You could Telnet to Ohio State's WHOIS and search for a person by name, and it would tell you their email address. But every university did it slightly differently, so you had to remember the right format for each one.

sections.title: Tools, Glossary, and Access Methods
sections.content:
The RFC includes a glossary of key technologies and tools for the early Internet:

  • BITNET: A separate network of mainframes and minicomputers connecting universities, offering email and file transfer but not Telnet.
  • FTP (File Transfer Protocol): The standard method for downloading files from remote computers. Anonymous FTP allowed public access without a login, using "anonymous" as the username and your email address as the password.
  • Telnet: For remote login to a computer. TN3270 was used for IBM mainframes with 3270 terminal emulation.
  • Listserv: A BITNET program for managing mailing lists and distributing files by email.

The RFC also mentions books worth reading for network managers, such as "Internetworking with TCP/IP" by Douglas Comer and "The Matrix" by John Quarterman. Finally, it lists periodicals available for free subscription (PC Week, MacWeek, Network World) that network managers could use to stay current.
sections.eli5: The RFC teaches you how to use the tools: FTP for getting files, Telnet for logging into remote computers, Listserv for mailing lists. It also lists books to read and magazines to subscribe to so you can learn more about networking.
